title: Network policy and PrivateLink

story: The broker has two doors. One faces the sandbox VMs: that is where Nova's harness asks it to push a branch or post in Slack, always inside the scope of its run. The other door is internal, and only the orchestrator should ever use it. Through that door, a request opens a new run's scope and gets back a fresh capability, the pass that lets a VM act for that run.

Now think about the n8n pod that shares the cluster with us, or a test service some other team deploys next month. Inside a Kubernetes cluster, every pod can open a connection to every other pod, unless someone says otherwise. So any of them can knock on the broker's internal door. The broker checks what it receives, but a door that strangers can reach is a door they can keep trying.
hook.question: How do we make sure that only the orchestrator can even open a connection to the broker's internal port?

read.h: Inside a cluster, everyone can talk
p: Kubernetes gives every pod an IP address and lets every pod reach every other pod, in any namespace, on any port. That makes the first deploy easy, and it is the opposite of what you know from AWS, where a security group refuses everything you did not allow. On inf it means the broker's internal port, the Temporal frontend and the gateway are all reachable from pods that have nothing to do with the agent platform.

A NetworkPolicy changes that for the pods it selects. It is an allow-list attached to pods by label. It has three parts: podSelector says which pods it protects, policyTypes says which direction it covers, Ingress for traffic coming into those pods and Egress for traffic going out of them, and the rules list who is allowed. The moment one policy selects a pod for a direction, everything in that direction that no rule allows is refused. Pods that no policy selects stay fully open.

code.text:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: broker
  namespace: ai-agents
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: broker
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: orchestrator-worker
      ports:
        - port: internal
    - ports:
        - port: sandbox

notes.text: The pods this policy protects: the broker's. From now on, any incoming connection that no rule below allows is refused.
Only incoming traffic is covered. The broker's own outgoing calls, to GitHub and its database, are not touched by this policy.
Rule one: only pods labelled app=orchestrator-worker in this namespace may connect…
…and only to the internal port. Ports can be named in the Deployment, so the policy does not repeat numbers.
Rule two has no from, so any source may use the sandbox port. The VMs arrive there through the load balancer described below.

read.h: A policy is a request; the network plugin enforces it
p: Kubernetes itself stores your NetworkPolicy but does not enforce it. The network plugin does, the software that gives pods their network, and some plugins ignore policies completely. A policy on such a cluster applies without any error and changes nothing, which is the worst kind of wall: one that only looks like a wall. So a policy is not finished when kubectl apply succeeds. It is finished when a probe from a pod that should be refused is refused, and a probe from the pod that should pass still passes. The k3s cluster in your lab enforces policies, so you can see both.

Selectors have one trap that people fall into again and again. Inside one from or to item, a namespaceSelector and a podSelector together mean both must match: pods with this label in that namespace. Written as two separate items in the list, they mean either one is enough, which can open the door to a whole namespace. The dash at the start of a line is the difference, so read every list slowly.

The policy below shows both shapes. It is an Egress policy, which limits where a pod may connect to, and it starts the way every egress policy must, by allowing DNS. Every call begins with a question to the cluster's DNS server, kube-dns, on port 53, and without this rule every request fails with "Resolving timed out", which looks like a network outage. You will meet exactly that error in the lab.

code.file: the start of every egress policy
code.text:
policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              k8s-app: kube-dns
      ports:
        - { port: 53, protocol: UDP }
        - { port: 53, protocol: TCP }
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: broker

notes.text: Every namespace gets the label kubernetes.io/metadata.name automatically, so you can select kube-system by name.
No dash before podSelector: it is in the same item as the namespaceSelector, so both must match. That means the DNS pods in kube-system, nothing else.
DNS uses UDP, and TCP for large answers. Allow both.
A new dash, so a new item: a second allowed destination, the broker pods in our own namespace.

deeper.h: Go deeper: names on the internet
p: Plain NetworkPolicy can name pods, namespaces and IP ranges, but not domain names such as slack.com. Our brain bot, for example, should talk only to Slack, GitHub, Jira and the LLM gateway. The gateway is a pod, so a podSelector works; the other three are on the internet, so allowing them needs their IP ranges, or a network plugin with its own domain rules. When a policy has to allow port 443 to anywhere for a while, say so in the pull request, so a reviewer sees the gap.

A NetworkPolicy works inside one cluster. The sandbox VMs are not in the cluster, though; they live in a separate AWS account, in a network with no route to inf. They still need three things on inf: the broker's sandbox door, the LLM gateway and the telemetry collector. Joining the two networks, which AWS calls peering, would make every address on inf reachable from every VM, including the broker's internal door and every internal tool.

PrivateLink is the same allow-list idea between accounts, and you met it in p4-5. We put one internal load balancer on inf with exactly three listeners, publish it as an endpoint service, and allow exactly one account, the sandboxes' account, to connect to it. In that account it appears as a private address with DNS names like broker.ai-agents.example.com. The broker's internal port is not in the list, so from a VM it does not exist at all. Inside the cluster the NetworkPolicy guards the internal door; between the accounts PrivateLink decides which doors exist.

code.file: the published side of the PrivateLink unit (shortened)

notes.text: The whole list of what a VM can reach on inf. A fourth entry would be a visible line in a reviewed plan.
No manual approval step, because the next lines already say who may connect.
One account, by its ID. A mistake in any other account's Terraform cannot connect to our services.

lab.title: Close the broker's internal door
needs: The laptop cluster from p5-1, running (docker start academy)
lab.goal: Show that every pod can reach the broker, then write a NetworkPolicy so only the orchestrator worker can, and prove it from three different pods.

guess.q: You apply a NetworkPolicy that selects the broker pods and allows ingress only from pods labelled app=orchestrator-worker. The Slack app's pod, in the same namespace, calls the broker. What happens?

options.text: It works, because pods in the same namespace always trust each other.
options.why: Namespaces are not walls by themselves. Once a policy selects the broker, only what a rule allows gets in, and the Slack app's label is not in the rule.

options.text: It is refused, because the Slack app's pod does not carry the label the rule allows.
options.why: The policy is an allow-list by label. Same namespace or not, only app=orchestrator-worker gets through.

options.text: Kubernetes refuses to start the Slack app's pod until a rule allows it.
options.why: Policies never stop pods from running. They only decide which connections are allowed.

follow.say: Start from clean namespaces: ai-agents for our services and n8n for a neighbour that shares the cluster.
follow.do: export KUBECONFIG=~/academy-k3s.yaml && kubectl delete namespace ai-agents n8n --ignore-not-found && kubectl create namespace ai-agents && kubectl create namespace n8n
follow.see:
namespace "ai-agents" deleted
namespace/ai-agents created
namespace/n8n created

follow.say: Start the broker with a Service, and three callers that only sleep, so you can run curl inside them: the orchestrator worker and the Slack app in ai-agents, and n8n in its own namespace.
follow.do: kubectl -n ai-agents create deployment broker --image=nginx:1.27 && kubectl -n ai-agents expose deployment broker --port=80 && kubectl -n ai-agents create deployment orchestrator-worker --image=curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -- sleep 86400 && kubectl -n ai-agents create deployment slack-app --image=curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -- sleep 86400 && kubectl -n n8n create deployment n8n --image=curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -- sleep 86400
follow.see:
deployment.apps/broker created
service/broker exposed
deployment.apps/orchestrator-worker created
deployment.apps/slack-app created
deployment.apps/n8n created

follow.say: Wait until all of them run, then call the broker from each caller. With no policy at all, expect everyone to get in.
follow.do: kubectl -n ai-agents wait deploy --all --for=condition=Available --timeout=120s && kubectl -n n8n wait deploy --all --for=condition=Available --timeout=120s && for t in n8n/n8n ai-agents/slack-app ai-agents/orchestrator-worker; do printf '%-30s' "$t"; kubectl -n ${t%/*} exec deploy/${t#*/} -- curl -s --max-time 3 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://broker.ai-agents 2>/dev/null; done
follow.see:
deployment.apps/broker condition met
…
n8n/n8n                       200
ai-agents/slack-app           200
ai-agents/orchestrator-worker 200

follow.say: Write the policy: it protects the broker pods and lets in only the orchestrator worker, on the broker's port.
follow.do:
cat > broker-policy.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: broker-internal-from-orchestrator
  namespace: ai-agents
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: broker
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: orchestrator-worker
      ports:
        - port: 80
EOF
kubectl apply -f broker-policy.yaml

follow.say: Run exactly the same calls again. 000 means curl got no HTTP answer at all: the connection was refused before it reached nginx.
follow.do: for t in n8n/n8n ai-agents/slack-app ai-agents/orchestrator-worker; do printf '%-30s' "$t"; kubectl -n ${t%/*} exec deploy/${t#*/} -- curl -s --max-time 3 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://broker.ai-agents 2>/dev/null; done

follow.say: Read the policy back the way Kubernetes understood it, because that is how you check a policy you did not write.
follow.do: kubectl -n ai-agents describe networkpolicy broker-internal-from-orchestrator | sed -n '/Spec:/,$p'
follow.see:
Spec:
  PodSelector:     app=broker
  Allowing ingress traffic:
    To Port: 80/TCP
    From:
      PodSelector: app=orchestrator-worker
  Not affecting egress traffic
  Policy Types: Ingress

lab.build: Our Temporal's frontend should be reachable from pods in ai-agents only. Run a stand-in: kubectl -n ai-agents create deployment temporal-frontend --image=nginx:1.27 and kubectl -n ai-agents expose deployment temporal-frontend --port=7233 --target-port=80. Write a NetworkPolicy temporal-frontend-from-ai-agents that protects the pods labelled app=temporal-frontend and allows ingress from every pod in the same namespace (an empty podSelector, {}). Prove it with the same loop, calling http://temporal-frontend.ai-agents:7233: n8n must get 000, the Slack app and the orchestrator worker 200. If everyone gets 000, look closely at which port your rule names: the Service listens on 7233, but the pod listens on 80.
checks: Before any policy, all three callers print 200 for the broker
After broker-policy.yaml, n8n and the Slack app print 000 and the orchestrator worker prints 200
kubectl -n ai-agents describe networkpolicy shows PodSelector app=broker and From PodSelector app=orchestrator-worker
For temporal-frontend, n8n prints 000 while the Slack app and the orchestrator worker print 200
After the fix, the orchestrator worker reaches the broker again with its egress policy still in place

solution.text:
kubectl -n ai-agents create deployment temporal-frontend --image=nginx:1.27
kubectl -n ai-agents expose deployment temporal-frontend --port=7233 --target-port=80

# temporal-policy.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: temporal-frontend-from-ai-agents
  namespace: ai-agents
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: temporal-frontend
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector: {}     # every pod in ai-agents, and only there
      ports:
        - port: 80            # the pod's port, not the Service's 7233

lab.fix: A teammate wanted the orchestrator worker to talk to the broker and nothing else, so they gave it an Egress policy that allows only the broker pods on port 80. Apply that yourself (podSelector app: orchestrator-worker, policyTypes [Egress], one to item with podSelector app: broker and port 80), then call the broker from the orchestrator worker with curl -sS so errors show. It now fails with curl: (28) Resolving timed out, although the broker allows it in. Find what the worker can no longer reach, and add the rule that brings the answer back to 200 without opening anything else.
explain: Before any policy, why could n8n, a pod in a different namespace, reach the broker at all?
The Slack app is in the same namespace as the broker. Why was it refused, and what would have to change for it to get in?
Inside the cluster a NetworkPolicy guards the internal port. What decides that a sandbox VM in the other AWS account cannot reach that port either?
lab.done: The same curl printed 200 for everyone before the policy and 200 only for the orchestrator worker after it, and you can explain why the VMs cannot see the internal port at all.

check.q: You add policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress] to the broker's policy, with ingress rules but no egress rules at all. What happens to the broker?

options.text: Nothing changes for outgoing traffic, because there are no egress rules
options.why: The opposite. Listing Egress with no rules means no outgoing connection is allowed: the broker can no longer reach GitHub, its database, or even DNS.

options.text: Kubernetes rejects the policy as incomplete
options.why: It is a valid object and applies without a warning. That is what makes this mistake so common.

options.text: The allowed callers still get in, but the broker cannot open any connection itself, not even to DNS
options.why: Each direction listed in policyTypes becomes an allow-list. An empty allow-list allows nothing.

check.q: You applied a policy that should block n8n from the broker, and kubectl said created. What proves the wall is real?

options.text: A curl from an n8n pod is refused, while a curl from the orchestrator worker still gets an answer
options.why: The network plugin enforces policies, and some plugins ignore them. Only a probe from both sides shows that this cluster really does.
That only shows the policy is stored. On a plugin that ignores policies, it is listed and does nothing.

options.text: kubectl describe shows the right selectors
options.why: It shows the policy says the right thing. Whether anything enforces it is a separate question.

check.q: Why do the sandbox VMs reach inf through PrivateLink instead of peering the two networks?

options.text: Peering does not work between two AWS accounts
options.why: It does. The problem is that it opens too much, not that it is impossible.

options.text: Peering would make every address on inf reachable from the VMs; PrivateLink publishes only three ports, to one account
options.why: It is the same allow-list idea as a NetworkPolicy: the broker's internal port, Temporal and the internal tools simply do not exist from a VM.
Speed is not the reason. The reason is what becomes reachable.

p: The agent services' NetworkPolicies come with their units. The broker's policy lets only orchestrator-worker reach its internal port, where runs are opened and capabilities minted, and leaves its sandbox port to the load balancer. Our Temporal's frontend stays a ClusterIP Service, and a policy lets only pods in the ai-agents namespace reach port 7233. The brain bot gets an egress-only policy to Slack, GitHub, the Jira site and the LLM gateway.

The PrivateLink unit, ai-agents/sandbox-privatelink/, builds the internal Network Load Balancer on inf with three TLS listeners, the broker's sandbox port, the gateway and the OTel collector, binds them to the pods, and publishes the endpoint service to the ai-agents account only. The account's own tree holds the interface endpoint and the private DNS names broker., gateway. and otel.ai-agents.example.com. Never on that list: the broker's internal port, Temporal and envoy-internal, the entry point for internal tools. The threat model checks these walls with drills.

tickets.why: The broker's policy, orchestrator-worker only on the internal port, and the PrivateLink unit with its three ports.
The policy that lets only ai-agents pods reach Temporal's frontend on 7233.
The brain bot's egress policy: Slack, GitHub, Jira and the gateway only.
The threat model that lists what a sandbox can and can never reach, and drills it.

words.plain: An allow-list attached to pods by label, saying who may connect to them or where they may connect.
Traffic coming into a pod, and traffic going out of it. A policy covers only the directions it lists.
The software that gives pods their network. It enforces NetworkPolicies, and some plugins ignore them.
An AWS feature that publishes one load balancer to another account as a private address, instead of joining the networks.

review.q: Write the broker's policy from memory: which pods it protects, which direction, and the two rules.
review.a: podSelector app=broker, policyTypes Ingress; rule one from podSelector app=orchestrator-worker to the internal port; rule two the sandbox port with no from.

review.q: A new egress policy makes every call from a pod fail with a name-resolution timeout. What is missing?
review.a: A rule that allows DNS: to the kube-dns pods in kube-system on port 53, UDP and TCP.

review.q: Name the three things a sandbox VM can reach on inf, and two things it can never reach.
review.a: The broker's sandbox port, the LLM gateway and the OTel collector. Never the broker's internal port, Temporal, or the other internal tools on inf.

remember: Inside a cluster everyone can talk until a NetworkPolicy says otherwise, so we allow-list by label and prove it with a probe; between accounts, PrivateLink publishes only the doors we name.
